title: Mental Models by Mohnish Pabrai at Heilbrunn Center for Graham and Dodd Investing on April 21, 2026
summary: At Columbia's Heilbrunn Center Pabrai presents 30 mental models for investing derived from Munger's latticework: underdose on Ben Graham, the 20-punch card, circle of competence, hold great businesses forever (never cut the flowers), shameless cloning, checklists, low-risk/high-uncertainty bets, and 'your deepest desire is your destiny'. He reveals that 70% of his portfolio is in three Turkish stocks, recounts buying a third of Reysas for $8 million at a $15 million market cap against $800 million liquidation value, and regrets selling Ferrari, Progressive and Goldman Sachs; Q&A covers why Turkey is easy and India hard, and his daughter's investing.

ideas.idea: Mental models must be adopted cult-like with full immersion; the bedrock model is 'take a simple idea and take it seriously', and if you have even a hundredth of a percent of doubt you are better off not touching it.
ideas.detail: Human brains evolved to see a distorted reality; 'aha' moments where the world works differently than you thought are the models that give an edge. Overlaying models yields Munger's Lollapalooza effect where 1 plus 1 becomes 11.

ideas.idea: Underdose on Ben Graham: keep his three ideas (Mr. Market serves you, margin of safety, buy stocks as businesses) and forget the rest of Security Analysis and The Intelligent Investor.
ideas.detail: Graham's model was seared by the Depression's 25% unemployment, unseen in almost a century; following it too rigorously hurt both Pabrai and Buffett. Take half a tablet once a week of Graham and overdose instead on Poor Charlie's Almanack, Phil Fisher and Pulak Prasad.

ideas.idea: The 20-punch card reminds you that great ideas are rare; a compounder shows up once every 5 or 10 years.
ideas.detail: If you could only ever buy 20 stocks you would become extremely careful; he admits later 'Swiss Army knife' models violate it.

ideas.idea: The size of the circle of competence is irrelevant; be an inch wide and a mile deep at its epicenter.
ideas.detail: John Arrillaga became a billionaire investing only in real estate within one mile of Stanford, knowing 50 years of rents on every building, staying under-levered and buying marquee properties in crises.

ideas.idea: An extremely high error rate is guaranteed; you can be wrong 80% of the time and still do extremely well because 4% of US companies delivered all stock market returns over 90 years.
ideas.detail: Templeton said the best analyst is wrong a third of the time; Buffett said 12 ideas in 58-60 years created Berkshire, a 4% hit rate. A 1970 Nifty 50 portfolio with 2% in Walmart and the other 98% going to zero still beats the S&P today because the flower was not cut.

ideas.idea: Circle the wagons: never sell a great business when fairly priced or overpriced, only when absolutely egregiously overpriced.
ideas.detail: Buffett's longest-held stock is Coca-Cola from 1988 (38 years), so his buy-and-hold journey started past his mid-50s; Pabrai wants students to start in their 20s. Munger: you get only three or four trips to the pie counter in a lifetime, so load up heavily when you get there.

ideas.idea: His most painful mistakes are great businesses he sold: nearly 1% of Ferrari bought for about $10 million, Progressive 25 years ago, and Goldman Sachs at $65 in the crisis.
ideas.detail: He paid an effective market cap under $1 billion for Ferrari; Buffett bought Goldman at $130 and Pabrai at half that, then sold for a good profit when he should never have sold. Even five years ago he did not understand these models.

ideas.idea: Litmus test for a manager with a multi-decade record: the top two or three positions should be 70-80% of the portfolio, and he cannot find anyone who passes.
ideas.detail: Managers who owned Constellation Software since its IPO (35% annualized for about 15 years) but cap positions at 10% are cutting the flowers and watering the weeds.

ideas.idea: Be a shameless cloner: not one idea in his portfolio is his own, and you would do extremely well limited to Value Investors Club write-ups, even just letters A through H.
ideas.detail: VIC was set up by Joel Greenblatt; DataRoma shows quarterly what the luminaries bought and sold. His latest cloned idea is Gimat Gross, 'Turkey's Costco'.

ideas.idea: History rhymes: no one is interested in Turkey, so 70% of his portfolio is in three Turkish stocks and he wants it to be two.
ideas.topic: Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US
ideas.detail: Turkey today resembles the US market from 1975 to 1985 when Coke traded at 7 times earnings. He is going all in on Turkey with no consideration of anything else.

ideas.idea: Reysas was a cigar butt that turned out to be a compounder: $8 million bought one-third of a company with a $15 million market cap and $800 million liquidation value in 2019.
ideas.detail: It rents warehouses to Amazon, IKEA, Carrefour, Toyota and Mercedes on 99% leased, inflation-indexed contracts, with $200 million of debt. He now owns over 40%; market cap is about $1.5 billion against $2.5 billion liquidation value, and he manages $1.3 billion. A 5% block bought for $1 million from a Templeton fund selling indiscriminately is now worth $125 million.

ideas.idea: If you cannot explain the thesis to a 10-year-old in three or four sentences, do not invest; and delete Excel, because if you cannot do the math quickly in your head it is a pass.
ideas.detail: He told Columbia students that the program makes them overdose on Excel and that his only use of it was the deep-well rope.

ideas.idea: You need a rope to get out of a deep well: a temporary reality distortion field is legitimate when everything is going wrong.
ideas.detail: His father went bankrupt nine times and paid an astrologer to describe a beautiful future as his rope. In the financial crisis Pabrai's fund fell 67% from $600 million to $200 million with no redemptions, and his rope was an Excel sheet of what he thought the companies were worth.

ideas.idea: Once a portfolio has escape velocity, let a winner become 80% of it; Nick Sleep's only error was selling half his Amazon for ASOS.
ideas.detail: Nick Sleep and Zach returned $2.5 billion in 2013-14 after UK regulators objected to concentration and put a third each in Amazon, Berkshire and Costco; anyone who followed beat every manager since. Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance teaches intense pursuit of quality, which those three businesses embody.

ideas.idea: A 213-question pre-investment checklist built from great investors' mistakes shows the three big failure causes are leverage, misunderstood moats and leadership or ownership problems.
ideas.detail: He studied why Buffett lost money on Dexter Shoes. Do not buy levered businesses and make sure you understand the business well.

ideas.idea: Read the footnotes, turn every page, and enjoy hunting for needles in haystacks as Buffett has done from age 12 to 95.
ideas.detail: Buffett collected discarded racetrack tickets at Aksarben at 12, found Western Insurance at $15 with $25 earnings in Moody's Manual at 23, and after 15-20 years reading the Japan Company Handbook bought five trading companies at 7-8% yields fully funded with yen borrowed at 0.5%; dividends doubled and stocks tripled. Seth Klarman named a horse 'Read the Footnotes'; Robert Caro, the best researcher and writer, turns every page of 50 million at the LBJ Library.

ideas.idea: Who we are is hard-coded by age 5, so parents should focus for the first six years, coach from 6 to 12, and after 12 control only who the child's friends are.
ideas.detail: After 12 children are influenced by friends; when a low-quality friend appears, make a major insertion and remove that friend regardless of collateral damage. Buffett at 95 is the same kid he was at 12.

ideas.idea: Your deepest desire is your destiny: you can have only one deep desire, and if you go all in you will find PE-of-1 stocks or compounders at under 2% of liquidation value.
ideas.detail: From the Upanishads, 2,700 years old. The first Turkish company he visited with Haydar was at a PE of 0.1, one month's earnings equal to the market cap, though it had too much hair even for him.

ideas.idea: Always have someone you trust to discuss investment ideas with, because your brain will convince you a bad idea is the best thing since sliced bread.
ideas.detail: Munger said it was not always Warren; he ordered Pabrai and Li Lu to lunch at least monthly, which they did at Din Tai Fung. Guy Spier serves the same role.

ideas.idea: The mistress always looks hotter than the wife but the wife is hotter: be extremely reluctant to switch a stock you own for one you are looking at.
ideas.detail: Your brain is lying to you; what you already own is awesome.

ideas.idea: Introduce randomness into your life; picking up a Peter Lynch book at a London airport in 1994 led him to Buffett and to starting a fund.
ideas.detail: He had never bought a stock; Lynch's reverential references sent him to the Berkshire letters and Buffett biographies. Munger told him many times to introduce randomness.

ideas.idea: Be a Swiss Army knife while waiting for compounders: spin-offs, uber-cannibals, spawners, arbitrage, and 'heads I win, tails I do not lose much' bets.
ideas.detail: Alpha Metallurgical Resources bought back 32% of its shares in four years versus Apple 11% and Microsoft 10%; Alphabet and Amazon are spawners; he owned Transocean while it acquires Valaris. IPSCO in 2003-04 at $40 with $15 cash and two years of $15 cash flows was a 10% position sold at $155 after a $160 Swedish bid; a post on X comparing Einhorn's CONSOL Energy bet to IPSCO led him to CONSOL and then to met coal.

ideas.idea: Low risk plus high uncertainty equals likely high reward, the opposite of what Wall Street pays up for; and do not skim off the top, use 0/6/25 fees.
ideas.detail: ADP has ultra-low uncertainty and is priced to perfection; he wants businesses where Wall Street cannot figure out the earnings. Buffett and Munger became friends partly over the 0/6/25 partnership structure; he has to skim now because of his ETF.

ideas.idea: Turkey is an easy market and India a hard one: Turkish float cycles every 17 days with no research, while India's 100-150 well-governed companies trade at 50-70 times earnings versus 4-7 times for the same quality in Turkey.
ideas.topic: Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US
ideas.detail: Turkish investors want to buy at 10 and sell at 3 for 10%; Buffett's quote that the market transfers wealth from the active to the inactive could not be truer there. Of 5,000 listed Indian companies only 100-150 have exceptional governance and smart investors crowd those names.

ideas.idea: He never talks to his kids about investing, but his daughter is already interested only in great businesses, though she pays too much.
ideas.detail: The apple falls directly under the tree; her favorite or second-favorite stock is Turkish Costco.
